before.title: Rectangular PEC reflection class: Fourier completeness, weak solutions and energy conservation
before.statement: Assume Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants. Define the reflection boundary class by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2,x_3$-walls, and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$; extend $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$, cyclically for $B_2,B_3$. Work on the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$ in the real $L^2$ fields with these parities and distributional $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$. For smooth fields the parity class gives $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Then: (i) the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in this class, and the class is complete for the $L^2$ pairing ([[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]); (ii) for every initial datum in the class there is a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the same class ([[def-distributional-derivative]]); (iii) the energy $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ is constant along the solution. This is an explicit weak PEC model; it supplies neither trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields nor completeness in lossy, open or non-rectangular guides.
before.strategy: The one-dimensional character system on the torus is complete for complex $L^2$ ([[thm-trigonometric-system-is-complete-in-l-two-of-the-torus]]) and its Fourier partial sums converge in mean square ([[thm-l-two-fourier-series-converges-in-mean-square]]). If an $L^2(Q)$ function is orthogonal to every product of characters, fix two indices and integrate against those two characters: Fubini and Cauchy-Schwarz ([[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]) make the remaining one-variable coefficient an $L^2$ function whose character coefficients all vanish, hence it is zero; repeating in the second and third coordinates on a single null set gives product completeness; orthogonality follows by iterated one-variable integration and Parseval by expanding the squared distance to a finite projection. Reflection parities force sine in odd coordinates and cosine in even coordinates; the trigonometric product modes are the paired $\pm k_j$ projections. For each torus wavevector $k_j=\pi n_j/L_j$ the Fourier coefficients satisfy the finite-dimensional constant-coefficient linear system $\widehat E_t=i(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}k\times\widehat B$, $\widehat B_t=-ik\times\widehat E$ with $k\cdot\widehat E=k\cdot\widehat B=0$. Identify the complex coefficient space with its finite-dimensional real and imaginary parts. The constant linear right-hand side is globally state-Lipschitz on all time and state space, so [[cor-globally-lipschitz-odes-have-global-solutions]] gives a unique global solution through the initial coefficients. Differentiating $\varepsilon|\widehat E|^2+|\widehat B|^2/\mu$ gives zero by the scalar triple-product identity and conjugation, so its weighted norm is preserved; the constrained subspace and the parity patterns are preserved because $k\cdot(k\times v)=0$ and curl maps the stated parities into each other. Solve all coefficients, truncate to finitely many wavevectors, and pass to the limit with Parseval: the weighted tail norm equals its initial value, so the finite solutions converge uniformly in time in $L^2$, and the limit is $C_tL^2$ and satisfies the equations in the distributional sense ([[def-distributional-derivative]]) after testing against smooth periodic compactly supported-in-time tests: on each compact time support, uniform $L^2$ convergence and Cauchy-Schwarz pass the field pairings against the test time derivatives and spatial curls to the limit. No absolute summability of test Fourier coefficients is needed. Uniqueness: a $C_tL^2$ weak solution has continuous Fourier coefficients whose distributional derivatives are the displayed continuous right-hand sides; for each coefficient $z(t)$ and its continuous right-hand side $g(t)$, subtract the classical primitive $G(t)=\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$. FTC gives $G'=g$, so $z-G$ has zero distributional derivative. [[thm-a-distribution-with-zero-derivatives-on-a-connected-open-set-is-constant]] on $\mathbb R$ makes this regular distribution constant; continuity makes the equality pointwise. Thus each coefficient is a classical solution of the displayed finite-dimensional ODE, and global ODE uniqueness with its given initial value identifies it. Product completeness then identifies the fields. Energy conservation passes to the limit in norm. Countable Choice covers the Fourier, Fubini, Hilbert-space and regular-distribution supplier contracts; the finite-dimensional modal equations require no extra choice premise.

before.title: Calculus of separated phasor fields: real-part derivative identities and amplitude injectivity
before.reference: core-conditional-proofs.md#K9; scaffold-added necessary prerequisite (see batch-35 notes)
before.strategy: Differentiate each component of $\operatorname{Re}(we^{i\theta})$ with $w=\tilde F_j$ by the product and chain rules for real and imaginary parts ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), using $\operatorname{Re}(i\zeta)=-\operatorname{Im}\zeta$ and $\operatorname{Re}(-i\zeta)=\operatorname{Im}\zeta$; assemble the divergence and curl componentwise. For (d), write $C=a+ib$ with real $a,b$; the two scalar equations $a\cos\varphi_j-b\sin\varphi_j=0$ ($j=1,2$) form a real $2\times2$ system of determinant $\sin(\varphi_1-\varphi_2)$ for each component, hence $a_j=b_j=0$. If $F=G$ on an open $U$, then for every $x_t$ in the projection the phases attained in the open fibres include two values whose difference is not in $\pi\mathbb Z$ (an open fibre contains points with any phase in an interval of positive length), so $\tilde F(x_t)=\tilde G(x_t)$. The projection of a nonempty open set is nonempty and open.

before.title: The sine and cosine systems are complete orthogonal systems of L^2 on an interval and on a rectangle
before.reference: completed-expansion-arguments.md#G2; scaffold-added necessary prerequisite (see batch-35 notes)
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $L>0$ and $R=(0,L_1)\times(0,L_2)$ with $L_1,L_2>0$.
(a) [One interval] The families $\{\cos(m\pi x/L)\}_{m\ge0}$ and $\{\sin(m\pi x/L)\}_{m\ge1}$ are orthogonal complete systems in the real Hilbert space $L^2(0,L)$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]): each is orthogonal, and its closed linear span is all of $L^2(0,L)$.
(b) [Rectangle] With $m,n$ ranging over $\mathbb N_0$ in cosine slots and over $\mathbb N_{\ge1}$ in sine slots, each of the four product families $\{\cos\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\cos\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$, $\{\cos\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\sin\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$, $\{\sin\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\cos\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$ and $\{\sin\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\sin\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\}$ is an orthogonal complete system in $L^2(R)$; in particular the Neumann family $\{h_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge0}$ and the Dirichlet family $\{e_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge1}$ of [[lem-em-rectangle-mode-profile-identities]] are orthogonal complete systems in $L^2(R)$.
before.strategy: (a) Rescale $x=L u/\pi$ to period $2\pi$ ([[thm-linear-change-of-variables-for-lebesgue-measure]]). For $f\in L^2(0,L)$ orthogonal to every $\cos(m\pi x/L)$, extend $f$ evenly to $(-L,L)$ and $2L$-periodically; the extended $F$ lies in $L^2$ of the torus and every character coefficient $\widehat F(k)$ is a fixed multiple of $\int_0^Lf(x)\cos(k\pi x/L)\,dx$, computed by splitting the integral at $0$ and substituting $x\mapsto-x$ on $(-L,0)$ ([[cor-c-one-change-of-variables-for-l-one-functions]]); hence all coefficients vanish and [[thm-trigonometric-system-is-complete-in-l-two-of-the-torus]] gives $F=0$, so $f=0$. The sine case uses the odd extension, whose character coefficients are the sine coefficients (the $k=0$ coefficient vanishes identically). (b) Orthogonality is product integration. If $f\in L^2(R)$ is orthogonal to every $c_m(x_1)d_n(x_2)$, then for each $m$ the function $g_m(x_2):=\int_0^{L_1}f(x_1,x_2)c_m(x_1)\,dx_1$ is in $L^2(0,L_2)$ by Cauchy-Schwarz and Fubini ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]), and $\int_0^{L_2}g_md_n=0$ for all $n$ by Fubini, so $g_m=0$ a.e. by (a). Taking the countable union of the exceptional null sets, for a.e. $x_2$ one has $\int_0^{L_1}f(x_1,x_2)c_m(x_1)\,dx_1=0$ for all $m$, so $f(\cdot,x_2)=0$ a.e. in $x_1$ by (a), and Fubini gives $f=0$ a.e. Completeness as closed span is therefore established; the orthogonal expansions converge in $L^2$ by [[thm-hilbert-space-fourier-expansion]]. The argument is symmetric in the four parity choices.

before.title: Rectangular PEC guide and cavity geometry, the zero-normal-B reflection class, and axis-relative TE/TM/TEM
before.statement:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, its SI units and its fields $E,B$ be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-si-conventions]] and [[def-em-fields]]. Fix $a,b>0$, write $x_t=(x_1,x_2)$, $e_z:=e_3$, and let $\nabla_t,\Delta_t,\operatorname{div}_t$ be the transverse gradient, Laplacian and divergence.
(a) [Straight guide] A straight guide region is $\Omega_A:=A\times\mathbb R$ for a bounded connected $C^1$ plane domain $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), with longitudinal axis $e_z$; for a rectangular cross-section $A=R_{ab}:=(0,a)\times(0,b)$ the region is called the rectangular guide and its walls are the four open faces $\{x_1=0\},\{x_1=a\},\{x_2=0\},\{x_2=b\}$. A rectangular cavity region is $\Omega_c:=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ for fixed $d>0$, with the six open faces as its walls. Spatial derivatives are taken at fixed $t$; the fields are defined on $\Omega\times I$ with the regularity declared by each theorem.
(b) [PEC boundary model] On every open wall (a wall minus its edges) the ideal perfectly conducting boundary model declares the two conditions $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$, where $n$ is the outward unit normal of that wall ($-e_1,+e_1,-e_2,+e_2$ on the four rectangular walls, and $\pm e_j$ on the six cavity walls). Its physical reading is the ideal-conductor limit of the stationary interface conditions of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]: with $E=B=0$ inside the ideal conductor the tangential electric field and the normal magnetic field vanish, while the surface-charge and surface-current readings $n\cdot D=\sigma_f$ and $n\times H=K_f$ are determined by the traces and are not prescribed here. The supplier's hypotheses (a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface with one-sided $C^1$ fields) cover a smooth stationary interface, not the $\sigma\to\infty$ idealization nor the box edges; the guide/cavity conditions on the open walls are therefore declared as an idealization of this definition, and no pointwise statement on the edges is made.
(c) [Zero-normal-B reflection class] For the rectangular box $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L=(a,b,d)$, the reflection class is the class of locally integrable fields $E,B$ on $Q$ whose extensions to the rectangular torus $\prod_j\mathbb R/(2L_j\mathbb Z)$, defined by extending $E_1$ evenly across the $x_1$-walls and oddly across the $x_2$-, $x_3$-walls and cyclically for $E_2,E_3$, and extending $B_1$ oddly across $x_1$ and evenly across $x_2,x_3$ and cyclically for $B_2,B_3$, are $L^2$ fields, together with the distributional constraints that $\operatorname{div}E$ and $\operatorname{div}B$ vanish on the torus for the extensions. This is the declared weak PEC model used for the cavity initial-value problem; for smooth fields the parities give $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ on $\partial Q$. Initial data not in this class (for example data with trapped normal $B$) are excluded, as are the general $H(\operatorname{curl})$ boundary classes, which are defined by the mathematical suppliers and are not identified here with the classical conditions.
(d) [TE, TM, TEM] For a guide or cavity field $(E,B)$, the longitudinal components are $E_z:=E\cdot e_z$ and $B_z:=B\cdot e_z$; the field is called TE (transverse electric) if $E_z\equiv0$, TM (transverse magnetic) if $B_z\equiv0$, and TEM if both vanish, always relative to the named axis $e_z$.
(e) [Separated phasor convention] For $\omega>0$ and $\beta\in\mathbb R$, a $\beta$-$\omega$ separated phasor field on the guide is a real field of the form $F(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\tilde F(x_1,x_2)e^{i(\beta x_3-\omega t)}\bigr)$ with a complex amplitude $\tilde F$, componentwise; $\omega/(2\pi)$ is the frequency and $\beta$ the longitudinal wave number, with $\beta>0$ describing propagation in the $+e_z$ direction under this phase convention.
(f) [Scope] The definition fixes the geometry, the PEC boundary model, the weak reflection class and the mode terminology; it asserts no field equation, no constitutive law and no existence or completeness of modes, and circular, non-rectangular, open-ended, junction and lossy guides or cavities are outside it.

before.title: Complete mode expansions of the declared guide and cavity classes: transverse profile completeness, the rectangular reflection class and the smooth PEC cavity eigenbasis
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the cited mathematical suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]), the lossless isotropic scalar constant branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ and $\sigma=0$, the macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] with $\rho_f=0$, $J_f=0$, and the guide, cavity, PEC and reflection-class conventions of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]].
(a) [Transverse profile completeness] For the cross-section $(0,a)\times(0,b)$, the families $\{h_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge0}$ and $\{e_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge1}$ of [[lem-em-rectangle-mode-profile-identities]] are orthogonal complete systems in $L^2$ of the rectangle ([[lem-em-rectangular-transverse-mode-completeness]]); hence the transverse scalar profiles of the TE and TM candidates of [[pthm-em-rectangular-mode-candidates]] exhaust the transverse $L^2$ profiles, with the orthogonal expansions converging in $L^2$.
(b) [Rectangular cavity reflection class] For the box $Q=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ with the reflection class and distributional constraints $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$ of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]](c): the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in the class at every time; every initial datum in the class has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of the lossless first-order system $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the same class, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]; along the solution the total stored energy $\int_Q u\,dx$ equals $\frac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ and is constant, where $u$ is the stored-energy density of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]]. For $C^1$-in-time solutions the four macroscopic equations with $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ hold distributionally.
(c) [Smooth PEC cavity] For a bounded $C^\infty$ cavity domain $\Omega$ and the PEC class $X,V,H$ of [[thm-em-waveguide-spectral-completeness]](a): the curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis $\{u_j\}$ with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity, $\lambda_j\to\infty$ whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and a finite-dimensional zero eigenspace that is retained; the eigen-equation $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ holds distributionally with the PEC trace, and each $u_j$ has a $C^\infty$ representative on the closure. For the first-order lossless system in this class the coefficients $a_j(t):=\langle E(\cdot,t),u_j\rangle$ of a smooth-in-time solution satisfy $a_j''+(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\lambda_ja_j=0$, the finitely many $\lambda_j=0$ coefficients are affine in $t$, and the finite-energy expansions converge in $C_tV\cap C_tH$ as in the cited supplier for the associated second-order wave.
(d) [Scope] The theorem asserts completeness only for the transverse $L^2$ profiles and for the two declared cavity classes with their exact hypotheses; it asserts no completeness for the unbounded guide's longitudinal expansion, and none for lossy, dispersive, open-ended, non-smooth, non-rectangular or exterior problems, no trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields, and no identification of the weak classes with every maximal tangential-trace realization. The zero eigenvalues and zero modes are retained throughout.

before.title: TEM modes of a coaxial guide and the single-conductor obstruction for harmonic transverse potentials
before.statement:
Assume the lossless isotropic scalar constant branch of [[post-em-material-closure]], the macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] with $\rho_f=0$, $J_f=0$, and the straight-guide, TEM and separated-phasor conventions of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]]; put $Z:=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$ and $v:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$.
(a) [Potential form] Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a bounded connected $C^1$ domain and let $\varphi\in C^2(\overline A;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$ (the plane Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]; a $C^2$ function with $\Delta\varphi=0$ is called harmonic). Define $\tilde E:=-\nabla\varphi$, $k:=\omega/v$ and $\tilde H:=\frac1Ze_z\times\tilde E$; then the separated real fields $E=\operatorname{Re}(\tilde Ee^{i(kx_3-\omega t)})$, $B=\mu\operatorname{Re}(\tilde He^{i(kx_3-\omega t)})$ satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations with $E_z=B_z=0$ (TEM), and the PEC condition on a smooth wall with unit normal $n$ is equivalent to $\partial_\tau\varphi=0$ along that boundary curve, so that $\varphi$ is constant on each connected component of $\partial A$. Moreover, if $A$ is star-shaped ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), every separated TEM phasor field on the guide is of this potential form: its transverse electric amplitude is closed and divergence-free, hence exact by [[cor-closed-exact-and-conservative-equivalence-on-star-shaped-domains]] applied to its real and imaginary parts separately, and the equations force $\tilde H=\frac1Ze_z\times\tilde E$ and $k=\omega/v$.
(b) [Single-conductor obstruction] If in the potential-form setting $\partial A$ is connected, then $\varphi$ is constant on $\partial A$, hence $\varphi$ is constant on $\overline A$ by the two-dimensional classical Dirichlet uniqueness of [[cor-classical-dirichlet-and-poisson-problems-are-unique]] (with the constant as the second solution), and therefore $\tilde E=\tilde H=0$: a single-conductor cross-section with connected boundary admits no nonzero TEM field in the potential form. In particular the rectangular guide of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]] (star-shaped, connected boundary) has no nonzero TEM candidate.
(c) [Coaxial example] Let $a<b$, $A:=\{x\in\mathbb R^2:a<|x|<b\}$ (two boundary components), fix $V\in\mathbb R$ and define $\varphi(x):=V\ln(b/|x|)/\ln(b/a)$, so that $\tilde E=V e_r/(|x|\ln(b/a))$ with $e_r:=x/|x|$ and $\tilde H=(V/(Z|x|\ln(b/a)))e_\varphi$ with $e_\varphi:=e_z\times e_r$. Then $\Delta\varphi=0$ on $A$: indeed $\partial_i\ln|x|=x_i/|x|^2$ by [[thm-logarithm-derivative-and-integral]] and the chain rule ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]), and the second partial derivatives sum to zero; hence $\varphi$ is constant on each boundary circle (values $V$ at $|x|=a$ and $0$ at $|x|=b$), the fields satisfy the source-free lossless macroscopic equations and the PEC conditions, and the relation $k=\omega/v$ is nondispersive with no cutoff. The amplitude integrals computed in polar coordinates with [[thm-polar-coordinates-formula-for-lebesgue-measure]] (the Jacobian factor $r$ is read from that formula) are $$W_e:=\tfrac12\varepsilon\int_A|\tilde E|^2\,dA=\tfrac12CV^2,\qquad W_m:=\tfrac12\mu\int_A|\tilde H|^2\,dA=\tfrac12CV^2,\qquad C:=\frac{2\pi\varepsilon}{\ln(b/a)};$$ the instantaneous per-length energies are $\tfrac12CV^2\cos^2\theta$ and $\tfrac12LI^2\cos^2\theta$ with $\theta=kx_3-\omega t$; equivalently, with $L:=\mu\ln(b/a)/(2\pi)$ and the boundary-current amplitude $I:=2\pi V/(Z\ln(b/a))$ one has $W_m=\tfrac12LI^2$ and $LC=\varepsilon\mu$. The two boundary components carrying distinct constants are exactly what the single-conductor obstruction excludes.
(d) [Scope] The obstruction clause (b) is proved for the potential form (equivalently, by (a), for star-shaped cross-sections); the general reduction of an arbitrary TEM field to the potential form on a merely simply connected non-star-shaped cross-section is not asserted here. The coaxial clause is an explicit conditional computation in the declared model with no empirical content; no lossy, radiation or signal-speed claim is made.
before.strategy: Clause (a): with $\tilde E=-\nabla\varphi$ the transverse curl vanishes and $\operatorname{div}\tilde E=-\Delta\varphi=0$; [[lem-em-separated-phasor-calculus]] reduces the four real equations to $\operatorname{curl}\tilde E=i\omega\mu\tilde H$, $\operatorname{curl}\tilde H=-i\omega\varepsilon\tilde E$, and substitution of $\tilde H=\frac1Ze_z\times\tilde E$ with $k=\omega/v$ verifies both by [[lem-em-transverse-vector-identities]](a). The boundary equivalence uses $n\cdot(e_z\times\tilde E)=\partial_\tau\varphi$ for the boundary tangent $\tau:=e_z\times n$ and the fundamental theorem along each connected boundary curve. In the star-shaped case, closedness of $\tilde E$ (forced by $\operatorname{curl}\tilde E=i\omega\mu\tilde H$ with $\tilde H_z=0$) makes it exact, and the transverse equations force $\tilde H$ and $k$ as displayed. Clause (b): constant $\varphi$ on the single boundary component, then Dirichlet uniqueness applied to $\varphi$ and the constant. Clause (c): $\Delta\varphi=0$ by the displayed direct differentiation; the radial integrals $\int_A|\tilde E|^2=\int_A|Z\tilde H|^2=2\pi V^2/\ln(b/a)$ are evaluated in polar coordinates; the constant $\varphi$ on each circle and the radial/tangential decomposition give the PEC conditions. Only the choice-free local clauses of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]] are used for the energy reading; no empirical premise is used.

before.title: Rectangular PEC reflection class: Fourier completeness, weak solutions and energy conservation
before.statement: Let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^3(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and let $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants. ## Statement

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $a < b$ and a function $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ continuous on $[a,b]$.

[L1] $[a,b]$ is closed and bounded, hence compact ([[def-interval]], [[def-open-and-closed-in-r]], [[def-bounded-set]], [[thm-heine-borel-characterisation-r]], [[def-open-cover-r]]).

[L2] A continuous real function on a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is bounded there ([[cor-boundedness-theorem-r]]).

[L3] Heine-Cantor: a continuous real function on a compact subset $K$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is uniformly continuous on $K$, that is, for every real $\eta > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ with $|f(x) - f(y)| < \eta$ for all $x, y \in K$ with $|x - y| < \delta$ ([[thm-heine-cantor-r]], [[def-uniform-continuity-real]]).

[L4] For a partition $P = (n,t)$ of $[a,b]$: $\Delta_i = t_{i+1} - t_i > 0$, $\sum_{i<n}\Delta_i = b-a$, and the uniform partition $U_N$ into $N \ge 1$ parts has every $\Delta_i$ equal to $(b-a)/\iota(N)$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]).

[L5] $U(f,P) - L(f,P) = \sum_{i<n}(M_i - m_i)\Delta_i$ and $M_i - m_i = \sup\{|f(x)-f(y)| : x, y \in I_i\}$ for bounded $f$ ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[L6] Riemann's criterion: a bounded $f$ is integrable if and only if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a partition $P$ with $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$ ([[thm-riemann-criterion]]).

[L7] For every real $\eta > 0$ there is a natural $N \ge 1$ with $1/\iota(N) < \eta$, and $\iota(N) > 0$ for $N \ge 1$ ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]], [[thm-of-archimedean]], [[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]).

[L8] Finite sums: scaling and monotonicity in the terms ([[def-finite-sum]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

[L9] Ordered-field arithmetic and the absolute value: adding a constant and multiplying by a positive quantity preserve an inequality; the order is total and transitive; $x, y \in [c,d]$ gives $|x - y| \le d - c$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[lem-of-add-order]], [[lem-of-sign-rules]], [[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-interval]]). These order-arithmetic facts are stated by their sources for the strict order only; the nonstrict forms used below follow by adjoining the equality case, in which the two sides coincide.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 $[a,b]$ is compact by [L1], so $f$ is bounded on $[a,b]$ by [L2] and its Darboux sums and integrals are defined. [given, L1, L2]

1.2 Let a real $\varepsilon > 0$ be given and put $\eta := \varepsilon \cdot \bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)^{-1}$, a positive real by [L9] since $b - a > 0$. [given, L9]

2.1 By [L3] applied to the compact set $[a,b]$ with this $\eta$, fix a real $\delta > 0$ such that $|f(x) - f(y)| < \eta$ for all $x, y \in [a,b]$ with $|x - y| < \delta$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L1, L3, choose]

3.1 By [L7] fix a natural $N \ge 1$ with $1/\iota(N) < \delta \cdot (b-a)^{-1}$, and put $P := U_N = (N,t)$, the uniform partition of $[a,b]$ into $N$ parts. Then every $\Delta_i$ equals $(b-a)/\iota(N) < \delta$ by [L4] and [L9]. [step 2.1, L4, L7, L9, choose]

4.1 For each $i < N$ and all $x, y \in I_i = [t_i, t_{i+1}]$ one has $|x-y| \le \Delta_i < \delta$ by [L9], hence $|f(x) - f(y)| < \eta$ by step 2.1. So $\eta$ is an upper bound of the set $\{|f(x)-f(y)| : x,y \in I_i\}$, and therefore $M_i - m_i \le \eta$ by [L5]. [step 2.1, step 3.1, L5, L9]

5.1 Consequently $U(f,P) - L(f,P) = \sum_{i<N}(M_i - m_i)\Delta_i \le \sum_{i<N}\eta\,\Delta_i = \eta\,(b-a) = \varepsilon \cdot 2^{-1} < \varepsilon$, using [L5], step 4.1, $\Delta_i > 0$, [L8], [L4] and [L9]. [step 4.1, L4, L5, L8, L9]

6.1 Since the real $\varepsilon > 0$ of step 1.2 was arbitrary and step 5.1 produced a partition with $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, criterion [L6] applies and $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$; it is bounded by step 1.1. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 5.1, L6] ∎

## Remarks

- **Continuity is sufficient and very far from necessary.** A monotone function may have infinitely many discontinuities and is still integrable ([[thm-monotone-implies-integrable]]); Thomae's function is discontinuous at every rational and integrable ([[cor-countably-many-discontinuities-integrable]]); and the indicator of the Cantor set is discontinuous at uncountably many points and integrable. The exact frontier is [[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

- **Where compactness enters, and what it buys.** Only through [L1], and then twice: [[cor-boundedness-theorem-r]] to know that the Darboux sums exist at all, and [[thm-heine-cantor-r]] to get one $\delta$ for the whole interval. On a non-compact interval both can fail: $x \mapsto 1/x$ is continuous on $(0,1)$ and unbounded there, so it has no Darboux sums at all.

- **Choice.** The proof selects nothing from an infinite family. The current proof of [[thm-heine-cantor-r]] also uses only a finite subcover, so this integrability argument is choice-free. See [[rem-riemann-integral-choice-ledger]].

## Statement

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Reals $a < b$, an integrable $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$, its integral function $F(x) = \int_a^x f$, a point $c \in [a,b]$ at which $f$ is continuous, and a real $\varepsilon > 0$.

[L1] $F(x) - F(c) = \int_c^x f$ for all $x, c \in [a,b]$, in either order ([[def-the-integral-function]], [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]).

[L2] Continuity at $c$: for every real $\eta > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that every $t \in [a,b]$ with $|t - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|f(t) - f(c)| < \eta$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

[L3] Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it, so $F'(c) = \lim_{x\to c} \bigl(F(x)-F(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$ is a meaningful symbol, the limit being taken over $[a,b]\setminus\{c\}$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-function-limit]], [[def-interval]]).

[L4] For $p < q$ in $[a,b]$: $f$ and $|f|$ and every constant are integrable on $[p,q]$; $\int_p^q \lambda = \lambda(q-p)$; sums and scalar multiples of integrable functions are integrable with the corresponding identity; and $\bigl|\int_p^q u\bigr| \le \int_p^q |u|$ ([[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]], [[lem-integral-elementary-bounds]], [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]], [[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]]).

[L5] If $u \le w$ pointwise on $[p,q]$ and both are integrable then $\int_p^q u \le \int_p^q w$ ([[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]]).

[L6] With oriented limits, $\int_q^p u = -\int_p^q u$ and $\int_p^p u = 0$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]).

[L7] Absolute value and ordered-field arithmetic: $|{-t}| = |t|$, $|t\,s| = |t||s|$, $|t| \le c$ follows from $-c \le t \le c$, a positive real has a positive inverse, and the order is total and transitive ([[lem-of-abs-value]], [[def-abs-value]], [[def-ordered-field]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]]). The nonstrict forms of the order facts follow from the strict ones by adjoining equality.

[L8] For every real $\eta > 0$ there is a real $\eta' > 0$ with $\eta' < \eta$ ([[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]], [[thm-of-archimedean]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [L2] with $\eta := \varepsilon \cdot 2^{-1}$, fix a real $\delta > 0$ such that $|f(t)-f(c)| < \varepsilon\cdot 2^{-1}$ for every $t \in [a,b]$ with $|t-c| < \delta$. [given, L2, L7, L8, choose]

1.2 For $x \in [a,b]$ with $x \ne c$, [L1] and [L4] give $F(x) - F(c) - f(c)(x-c) = \int_c^x f - \int_c^x f(c) = \int_c^x \bigl(f(t) - f(c)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t$, the constant $f(c)$ having integral $f(c)(x-c)$ over the oriented interval from $c$ to $x$ by [L4] and [L6]. [L1, L4, L6]

2.1 **The estimate for $c < x < c+\delta$.** Every $t \in [c,x]$ has $|t-c| < \delta$, so $-\varepsilon\cdot2^{-1} \le f(t)-f(c) \le \varepsilon\cdot 2^{-1}$ there by step 1.1, whence $\bigl|\int_c^x (f - f(c))\bigr| \le \varepsilon\cdot2^{-1}\,(x-c)$ by [L4] and [L5]. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L4, L5, L7]

2.2 **The estimate for $c-\delta < x < c$.** By [L6], $\int_c^x (f-f(c)) = -\int_x^c (f-f(c))$, and every $t \in [x,c]$ has $|t-c| < \delta$, so the same argument gives $\bigl|\int_c^x (f-f(c))\bigr| \le \varepsilon\cdot 2^{-1}\,(c-x)$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, L4, L5, L6, L7]

3.1 In both cases $\bigl|\int_c^x(f-f(c))\bigr| \le \varepsilon\cdot 2^{-1}\,|x-c|$, so dividing by the nonzero $|x-c|$ and using step 1.2 gives $\Bigl|\dfrac{F(x)-F(c)}{x-c} - f(c)\Bigr| \le \varepsilon\cdot 2^{-1} < \varepsilon$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ with $0 < |x-c| < \delta$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, L7]

4.1 Since $\varepsilon > 0$ was arbitrary, the limit of the difference quotient of $F$ at $c$ exists and equals $f(c)$ by [L3]; that is, $F'(c) = f(c)$. [step 1.1, step 3.1, L3]

5.1 If $f$ is continuous at every point of $[a,b]$ then step 4.1 applies at every $c \in [a,b]$, so $F' = f$ on $[a,b]$ and $F$ is a primitive of $f$. [step 4.1, L3] ∎

## Remarks

- **The estimate is written out for $x < c$ as well, and that is not redundancy.** For $x < c$ the factor $1/(x-c)$ is negative and the naive chain $m(x-c) \le \int_c^x \le M(x-c)$ reverses; what makes the argument uniform is taking absolute values *before* dividing, which is what steps 2.1, 2.2 and 3.1 do. This is the single most common error in this proof.

- **The route is the definition of the derivative, not the mean value theorem for integrals.** Deducing $F'(c) = f(c)$ from [[thm-first-mean-value-theorem-for-integrals]] would need $f$ continuous on a whole subinterval around $c$, which is a strictly stronger hypothesis than continuity at the single point $c$. The theorem as stated is the sharp one.

- **What is proved at a point is proved at a point.** Nothing here says $F$ is differentiable anywhere else, and nothing says $F' = f$ off the continuity set of $f$. Where $f$ is merely integrable, all that survives is [[thm-the-integral-function-is-lipschitz]].

- **Forward references, orientation only.** The two failures at a discontinuity are worked out on the companion page as [[cex-an-integrable-function-with-no-primitive]] and [[fs-the-integral-function-is-always-a-primitive]]; nothing above depends on either.

## Statement

Distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta u=\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u$ and are continuous linear maps on $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ for both the weak and strong distribution topologies. These claims hold in ZF. Assuming Countable Choice for the cited Riemann-to-Lebesgue comparison, if $f\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $|\alpha|\le k$, then $\partial^\alpha u_f=u_{\partial^\alpha f}$. In particular distributional differentiation extends classical smooth differentiation.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] Derivatives are signed transposes of test derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

[F2] Weak seminorms test one function, and strong seminorms test bounded sets ([[def-weak-and-strong-topologies-on-distributions]]).

[F3] Test differentiation is continuous and preserves compact supports with $p_m(\partial^\alpha\varphi)\le p_{m+|\alpha|}(\varphi)$ ([[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]).

[F4] Smooth mixed partials commute ([[thm-symmetry-of-higher-mixed-partials]]).

[F5] Regular functionals pair by the bilinear Lebesgue integral ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]).

[F6] Compact sets admit smooth compact cutoffs equal to one near them ([[lem-test-function-cutoffs-and-euclidean-localization]]).

[F7] One-dimensional integration by parts holds when the factors and their derivatives are continuous on a closed interval ([[thm-integration-by-parts]]).

[F8] For Riemann-integrable functions on boxes with integrable sections, iterated and multiple Riemann integrals agree ([[thm-riemann-fubini-on-product-rectangles]]).

[F9] Under Countable Choice, a bounded Borel Riemann-integrable real function on a nondegenerate box has the same Lebesgue integral ([[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]).

[F10] Countable Choice, needed only for the classical-compatibility clause below, is [[def-countable-choice]].

## Proof

**Given:** a distribution $u$ and multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$.

1.1 Evaluating consecutive derivatives on a test gives $(-1)^{|\alpha|+|\beta|}u(\partial^\beta\partial^\alpha\varphi)$. By F4 this is $(-1)^{|\alpha+\beta|}u(\partial^{\alpha+\beta}\varphi)$, which is $\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u(\varphi)$ by F1. Linearity follows from the same formula. [given, F1, F4]

2.1 For a single test $\varphi$, the weak seminorm of $\partial^\alpha u$ equals $|u(\partial^\alpha\varphi)|$, a weak seminorm of $u$. For a bounded test set $B$, the set $\partial^\alpha B$ is bounded: any zero-neighborhood has a zero-neighborhood inverse image under the continuous linear test derivative of F3, and absorption of $B$ by that inverse image gives absorption of its image. Hence $p_B(\partial^\alpha u)=p_{\partial^\alpha B}(u)$, a strong seminorm. These equalities prove continuity in both topologies, including for nets, without choice. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3]

3.1 Now assume F10 and $f\in C^1(\Omega;\mathbb C)$, and fix a test $\varphi$. Use F6 to choose $\chi=1$ near $\operatorname{supp}\varphi$ with compact support in $\Omega$. Extend $g=\chi f$ by zero to $\mathbb R^n$; it is $C^1$ because it vanishes near the complement of $\Omega$. Choose a nondegenerate box containing the supports of $g$ and $\varphi$ in its interior. On each coordinate segment F7 gives $\int g\partial_i\varphi=-\int(\partial_i g)\varphi$, because $\varphi$ is zero at both endpoints. For complex functions expand into real and imaginary parts and apply the real identity to the four products. All integrands and sections are continuous on compact boxes and are Riemann integrable: uniform continuity makes their oscillation Darboux sums arbitrarily small on sufficiently fine uniform grids. For $n>1$, F8 integrates the one-coordinate identity over the remaining coordinates; for $n=1$ this is already the required identity. F9 componentwise converts the two multiple Riemann integrals to Lebesgue integrals. Near the test support $g=f$ and $\partial_i g=\partial_i f$, so the resulting equality is $-\int_\Omega f\partial_i\varphi=\int_\Omega(\partial_i f)\varphi$. [step 2.1, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10]

snapshot.statement:

Let the PEC classes be those of [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]]: for a bounded $C^\infty$ domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$, $X$ is the graph-norm closure in $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$ of the smooth fields on the closure with $n\times u=0$, $V=\{u\in X:\operatorname{div}u=0\}$ and $H=\overline V^{\,L^2}$. Then:
(a) **Smooth cavity.** The curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis $\{u_j\}$ with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity, $\lambda_j\to\infty$ whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and a finite-dimensional zero eigenspace that is retained; the eigen-equation $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ holds distributionally with the PEC trace. For every chosen positive mathematical speed $v_{\mathrm{wave}}>0$ and every displacement datum $q_0\in V$ and velocity datum $q_1\in H$, the associated second-order wave has coefficients $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$. Displacement lies in $C(\mathbb R;V)$, velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$, and finite modal sums converge in these respective norms uniformly on compact time intervals. The finitely many $\lambda=0$ modes remain $a_j(t)=a_j(0)+ta_j'(0)$. The speed is a positive abstract parameter and has no physical dependency. The eigenfields are $C^\infty$ on the closure by [[lem-em-pec-cavity-eigenfield-boundary-regularity]], applied to the full-$X$ eigenvariational identity of the cavity supplier. The shifted scalar auxiliary boundary problems are solvable on the declared bounded smooth domain by [[thm-em-elliptic-boundary-existence]]; the specific scalar Dirichlet resolvent and its smooth-zero-boundary test density used in G3 are supplied by its recorded local resolvent lemma.
(b) **Rectangular class.** For every rectangular box $Q=\prod_j(0,L_j)$ with $L_j>0$ and every pair of positive mathematical coefficients $\varepsilon,\mu>0$, the separable products described in the mode verification are dense in the reflection-parity energy class, and every initial datum of that class has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the class with constant energy, with finite separated modes dense at every time. The rectangular statements are the recorded rectangular reflection-class completeness lemma [[lem-em-rectangular-pec-energy-completeness]] (the $G2$ branch); the individual TE/TM mode verification against the Maxwell equations and the PEC conditions is the recorded $G1$ physics branch, homed on the physical guide page and not consumed here as a mathematical premise. snapshot.title: Complete mode expansions of the declared guide and cavity classes: transverse profile completeness, the rectangular reflection class and the smooth PEC cavity eigenbasis
snapshot.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice as declared by the cited mathematical suppliers ([[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]), the lossless isotropic scalar constant branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ and $\sigma=0$, the source-free smooth macroscopic equations of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]] in the smooth branches, with $\rho_f=0$, $J_f=0$, and the explicitly declared weak first-order material equations in the weak cavity branches below, and the guide, cavity, PEC and reflection-class conventions of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]].
(a) [Transverse profile completeness] For the cross-section $(0,a)\times(0,b)$, the families $\{h_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge0}$ and $\{e_{mn}\}_{m,n\ge1}$ of [[lem-em-rectangle-mode-profile-identities]] are orthogonal complete systems in $L^2$ of the rectangle ([[lem-em-rectangular-transverse-mode-completeness]]); The full scalar Neumann and Dirichlet families have these $L^2$ expansions. The physical TE candidate family excludes $h_{00}=1$ by the full Maxwell equations: the remaining $h_{mn}$ are complete in the zero-mean subspace $\{f\in L^2:\int_Rf=0\}$, not in all scalar $L^2$. The Dirichlet TM profiles retain their full scalar completeness. The constant Neumann scalar profile is retained in the mathematical basis but is not asserted to be a nonzero positive-frequency TE mode.
(b) [Rectangular cavity reflection class] For the box $Q=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ with the reflection class and distributional constraints $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$ of [[def-em-guide-cavity-geometry]](c): the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in the class at every time; every initial datum in the class has a unique $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution of the lossless first-order system $\partial_tE=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{curl}B$, $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ in the same class, with derivatives as in [[def-distributional-derivative]]; this lossless first-order distributional system is the explicitly adopted weak material evolution of the reflection model, not inferred from the smooth-only hypotheses of [[pthm-em-macroscopic-maxwell]]; along the solution the total stored energy $\int_Q u\,dx$ equals $\frac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ and is constant, where the weak stored-energy density is defined almost everywhere by this nonnegative quadratic expression, consistent with the smooth local definition of [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]]. Its integrability and constancy are furnished by the mathematical reflection-class energy result; no nonlinear weak Poynting identity is asserted. For $C^1$-in-time solutions the four macroscopic equations with $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ hold distributionally.
(c) [Smooth PEC cavity] For a bounded $C^\infty$ cavity domain $\Omega$ and the PEC class $X,V,H$ of [[thm-em-waveguide-spectral-completeness]](a): the curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis $\{u_j\}$ with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity, $\lambda_j\to\infty$ whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and a finite-dimensional zero eigenspace that is retained; the eigen-equation $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ holds distributionally with the PEC trace, and each $u_j$ has a $C^\infty$ representative on the closure. Put $v_{\mathrm{wave}}=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}>0$. The associated second-order electric wave has the full supplied interface: for arbitrary initial displacement in $V$ and velocity in $H$, its displacement is in $C(\mathbb R;V)$, its velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$, and finite modal sums converge in these respective norms uniformly on compact time intervals. Its zero eigenmodes may be affine in time. Separately, let $J$ be an open time interval and let a strong first-order solution obey $E\in C^1(J;H)\cap C(J;V)$ and $B\in C^1(J;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(J;H(\operatorname{curl}))$, with the first-order equations as $L^2$ identities and both distributional divergence constraints. Electric tangential-zero boundary data are encoded by $E(t)\in V$. The magnetic normal-zero condition is declared weakly by $\int_\Omega B(t)\cdot\nabla\psi=0$ for every smooth scalar $\psi$ on the closure; when $B\in C^1(\overline\Omega)$ this is $n\cdot B=0$, using $\operatorname{div}B=0$. No magnetic membership in the electric tangential-zero class $X$ is assumed. Then $a_j(t):=\langle E(t),u_j\rangle$ is $C^2$ and satisfies $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$. For $\lambda_j=0$, the admissible first-order coefficients satisfy $a_j'=0$ and are constant, with the zero eigenfields retained. This extra compatibility distinguishes first-order Maxwell data from arbitrary second-order $V\times H$ data; it does not remove the broader supplied second-order wave or its affine zero modes.
(d) [Scope] The theorem asserts completeness only for the transverse $L^2$ profiles and for the two declared cavity classes with their exact hypotheses; it asserts no completeness for the unbounded guide's longitudinal expansion, and none for lossy, dispersive, open-ended, non-smooth or exterior problems, or arbitrary non-rectangular guide problems beyond the explicitly declared smooth-cavity spectral class, no trace regularity for arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ fields, and no identification of the weak classes with every maximal tangential-trace realization. The zero eigenvalues and zero modes are retained throughout.
snapshot.strategy: Clause (a) is [[lem-em-rectangular-transverse-mode-completeness]](b) instantiated at the cross-section, whose profiles are those of the candidate theorem. Clause (b) is the rectangular reflection-class lemma [[lem-em-rectangular-pec-energy-completeness]] read physically, as packaged in [[thm-em-waveguide-spectral-completeness]](b): the class, the first-order system, density of finite separated modes, unique $C_tL^2$ weak solutions and constant energy all come from that supplier; the identification of the energy with $\int_Qu$ uses $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ and [[pthm-em-restricted-material-energy]](a), and the macroscopic equations follow from the two evolution equations together with the distributional divergence constraints of the class. For the scalar basis distinction in (a), every nonconstant Neumann product is orthogonal to $h_{00}=1$, and the complete orthogonal expansion of [[lem-em-rectangular-transverse-mode-completeness]] shows that deleting that one basis element gives precisely its orthogonal complement, the zero-mean subspace. The constant scalar element remains in the full basis and is excluded only as a monochromatic TE reconstruction. In (b), the explicit weak first-order model is solved by [[lem-em-rectangular-pec-energy-completeness]] as packaged in the wrapper; its Fourier energy proof gives the quadratic energy conservation without applying a smooth-only local balance to rough fields. For (c), [[thm-em-waveguide-spectral-completeness]] supplies the spectral and smooth-eigenfield assertions and the associated wave at the positive parameter $v_{\mathrm{wave}}=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}$, with its exact arbitrary $V\times H$ initial-data interface, displacement $C_tV$ and velocity $C_tH$. To derive the first-order coefficient equations, prove the actual curl pairing against each smooth PEC eigenfield $u_j$, not an unproved equality of electric and magnetic boundary classes. A smooth normal collar of the compact boundary exists by [[thm-euclidean-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem]]. Write $s$ for the inward normal coordinate (its gradient is the negative extended unit normal) and use the standard smooth step [[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]] to set a cutoff $\eta_\delta=0$ for $s\le\delta$ and $1$ for $s\ge2\delta$. The normal tube has bounded Jacobians on the compact collar. Since $n\times u_j=0$ on the boundary and $u_j$ is smooth, $|n\times u_j|\le Cs$ in the collar. Thus $\eta_\delta u_j\to u_j$ and $\operatorname{curl}(\eta_\delta u_j)\to\operatorname{curl}u_j$ in $L^2$: the derivative-cutoff term is bounded on a layer of volume $O(\delta)$ because $|\nabla\eta_\delta|\le C/\delta$ and its cross product with $u_j$ is $O(s/\delta)$. For every $F\in H(\operatorname{curl})$, the distributional identity on the compactly supported smooth test $\eta_\delta u_j$ is $\langle\operatorname{curl}F,\eta_\delta u_j\rangle=\langle F,\operatorname{curl}(\eta_\delta u_j)\rangle$. Cauchy-Schwarz and the two $L^2$ limits give $\langle\operatorname{curl}F,u_j\rangle=\langle F,\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle$. Apply this only to $F=B(t)$, which has the stated actual graph regularity. Then $a_j'=v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\langle B,\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle$. The assumed $B\in C^1_tL^2$ permits one further scalar derivative, giving $a_j''=v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\langle B',\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle=-v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\langle\operatorname{curl}E,\operatorname{curl}u_j\rangle=-v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_j\langle E,u_j\rangle$ by the full-$X$ eigenvariational identity of [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]], since $E(t)\in V\subset X$. No second time derivative of the whole field is assumed. If $\lambda_j=0$, that identity tested at $u_j$ gives $\operatorname{curl}u_j=0$, so the preceding formula for $a_j'$ is zero. Such electric zero modes are constant under first-order Maxwell evolution, while the associated unrestricted second-order equation retains affine zero modes. Divergence constraints and the declared magnetic normal condition remain part of the physical model; the pairing does not impose a magnetic electric-type trace. The inherited AC and AComega assumptions cover the spectral/Fourier and collar suppliers. No lossy or open-domain step is made.

snapshot.statement: Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Three exact boundary checks. (i) The sphere trace $f(n)=n_3$ is the trace of the homogeneous degree-one harmonic polynomial $u(x)=x_3$, so the ball boundary branch of [[thm-em-spherical-multipole-basis]] applies to it; the simultaneous conditions $\Delta u=0$ in the unit ball $B_1$ and $\partial_nu=1$ on $S^2$ are incompatible, because the divergence theorem gives $0=\int_{B_1}\Delta u\,dx=\int_{S^2}\partial_nu\,d\sigma=\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$. snapshot.title: Outgoing DtN coefficient at degree zero and the explicit PEC topology zero mode
snapshot.statement: (i) At degree $l=0$ the outgoing radial function of the spherical Hankel lemma is $h_0(z)=-ie^{iz}/z$, so for $k,R>0$ the Dirichlet-to-Neumann coefficient ([[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]]) is $t_0=kh_0'(kR)/h_0(kR)=ik-1/R$: its real part $-1/R$ is negative and its imaginary part $k$ is positive, as the spherical trace lemma requires. (ii) In the spherical shell $a<|x|<b$, the field $u(x)=\operatorname{grad}|x|^{-1}=-x/|x|^3$ is smooth on the closure, nonzero, normal to both boundary spheres, curl-free and divergence-free: $u=\nabla\Phi$ with $\Phi(x)=|x|^{-1}$ harmonic off the origin, so $\operatorname{curl}u=\operatorname{curl}\nabla\Phi=0$ and $\operatorname{div}u=\Delta\Phi=0$ there ([[thm-the-curl-of-a-gradient-vanishes]], [[lem-laplace-fundamental-solution-is-harmonic-off-its-pole]]). Thus $u$ lies in the PEC class $X$ of the cavity spectral lemma ([[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]]) with zero curl, and it has zero curl eigenvalue: eliminating all topology zero modes would incorrectly discard this explicit admissible vector field.
snapshot.strategy: (i) Direct computation: with $h_0(z)=-ie^{iz}/z$, logarithmic differentiation using the algebra of derivatives and the derivative of the complex exponential ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]) gives $h_0'(z)=h_0(z)\,(i-1/z)$, hence $kh_0'(kR)/h_0(kR)=ik-1/R$ with real part $-1/R<0$ and imaginary part $k>0$; both agree with the exact bounds of the spherical Hankel lemma ([[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]]). (ii) The field $-x/|x|^3$ equals the gradient of $|x|^{-1}$ off the origin; the curl of a gradient vanishes ([[thm-the-curl-of-a-gradient-vanishes]]) and its divergence is the Laplacian of the fundamental solution, which vanishes off the pole ([[lem-laplace-fundamental-solution-is-harmonic-off-its-pole]]); on each boundary sphere $|x|=c$ the field $-x/c^3$ is a nonzero multiple of the outward normal, so its tangential part is zero and it belongs to the weak PEC class of the cavity lemma ([[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]]); its curl is zero pointwise, so it is a nonzero vector in the kernel of the curl form, and such a vector is exactly a zero eigenvalue solution that any complete spectral description of the PEC class must retain.

snapshot.title: A rectangular-cavity standing mode at resonance: explicit fields and the PEC end-cap check
snapshot.statement: Let $a,b,d>0$ and $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ be constants, put $E_{\mathrm{sp}}(x):=e_1\sin\frac{\pi x_2}{b}\sin\frac{\pi x_3}{d}$, and for $\omega>0$ define $E(x,t):=E_{\mathrm{sp}}(x)\cos(\omega t)$ and $B(x,t):=-\frac1\omega(\operatorname{curl}E_{\mathrm{sp}})(x)\sin(\omega t)$, where the curl is the fixed-time spatial curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Then $E,B$ are smooth, $\operatorname{div}E_{\mathrm{sp}}=0$, $\Delta E_{\mathrm{sp}}=-[(\pi/b)^2+(\pi/d)^2]E_{\mathrm{sp}}$, and $E,B$ satisfy the four source-free macroscopic equations on the box $\Omega_c=(0,a)\times(0,b)\times(0,d)$ in the lossless isotropic scalar branch exactly when $$\omega^2=\frac{1}{\varepsilon\mu}\Bigl[\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{b}\Bigr)^2+\Bigl(\frac{\pi}{d}\Bigr)^2\Bigr];$$ with that resonance, $n\times E=0$ and $n\cdot B=0$ hold on all six walls, so $(E,B)$ is a PEC cavity mode. It is the cutoff instance $\beta=0$ of the TM family of [[pthm-em-rectangular-mode-candidates]](b) taken with axis $e_1$, cross-section $(0,b)\times(0,d)$ and indices $(m,n)=(1,1)$: the field is independent of $x_1$, which is why it also satisfies the $x_1=0$ and $x_1=a$ end-cap conditions for every box length $a>0$. The example asserts a conditional model solution, not an observed resonance.
snapshot.strategy: By [[lem-em-transverse-vector-identities]](b), $\operatorname{curl}(e_1e_{11})=-e_1\times\nabla e_{11}$ is $x_1$-independent and divergence-free, and $E=E_{\mathrm{sp}}\cos\omega t$, $B=-\frac1\omega\operatorname{curl}E_{\mathrm{sp}}\sin\omega t$ arise from the TM amplitudes with $\beta=0$ and $e_{11}=\sin\frac{\pi x_2}{b}\sin\frac{\pi x_3}{d}$ (at $\beta=0$ the transverse electric amplitude vanishes and $\tilde H=\frac{i\omega\varepsilon}{k_c^2}e_1\times\nabla e_{11}$ is imaginary, giving the $\sin\omega t$ field). The resonance condition is exactly $k_{11}^2=\omega^2\varepsilon\mu$ with $k_{11}^2=(\pi/b)^2+(\pi/d)^2$ from [[lem-em-rectangle-mode-profile-identities]](a). By the candidate theorem the fields satisfy the four equations and the guide wall conditions on the four faces with normals $\pm e_2,\pm e_3$; the amplitudes are independent of $x_1$, so $n\times E=e_1\times E$ and $n\cdot B=B_1$ vanish on $x_1=0,a$ as well, giving the cavity conditions. The magnetic partner is fixed by $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ with the displayed sign. No empirical premise is used.

snapshot.title: Existence and uniqueness for the smooth exterior vector Helmholtz mixed boundary problem
snapshot.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice inherited from the explicitly used variational, Sobolev and compact-spectral suppliers (and, for the exterior branch, the Fredholm alternative). Let $O\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set with $C^\infty$ boundary, let $D=\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline O$ be connected, let $k>0$, and let $R>0$ with $\overline O\subset B_R(0)$. For every smooth tangent field $e_T$ on $\partial O$ there is exactly one field $E$, $C^\infty$ on $\overline D$, satisfying, with the Euclidean Laplacian acting componentwise ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]),
$$(\Delta+k^2)E=0\ \text{ on }D,\qquad \operatorname{div}E=0\ \text{ on }D,\qquad E_{\text{tangential}}=e_T\ \text{ on }\partial O,$$
and outgoing on the large sphere $S_R$ in the modal sense of [[lem-em-sphere-outgoing-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]. Given the prescribed tangential trace and $\operatorname{div}E=0$, the corresponding normal closure is the relation $\partial_nE_n+(\operatorname{div}n)E_n=-\operatorname{div}_{\partial O}e_T$ with $n$ the outward normal of the truncated exterior region $B_R\setminus\overline O$ (pointing into $O$ on the inner boundary). This is the explicit Maxwell boundary closure used by the PEC scattering consumer; three independent scalar Dirichlet data are not asserted to be equivalent.

On the truncated annulus $A=B_R\setminus\overline O$ introduce $X=\{v\in H^1(A;\mathbb C^3):v_{	ext{tangential}}=0	ext{ on }\partial O\}$, a closed subspace of $H^1$ by the trace continuity of [[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]]; the trace machinery is smooth for the classical solutions. With $\kappa=\operatorname{div}n$ on the inner boundary, the form
$$a(E,v)=\int_A igl(
abla E:\overline{
abla v}-k^2E\cdot\overline v igr)+\int_{\partial O}\kappa E_n\overline{v_n}-\langle T_RE,vangle_{S_R}$$
is bounded on $H^1$ by [[lem-em-sphere-outgoing-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]] and bounded $\kappa$. Its real part is coercive after shifting by a real $\lambda>k^2+C_\delta+1$: the outer term is nonnegative by the sign of $\operatorname{Re}T_R$, and the curvature term is absorbed by the collar inequality proved in [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]] with $2ab\le\delta a^2+\delta^{-1}b^2$. The complex coercive form is inverted by the explicit contraction iteration (Hilbert Riesz representation [[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]] turns the shifted form into a bounded operator $B$ with $\operatorname{Re}\langle Bx,xangle\ge\alpha\|x\|^2$; for small $t>0$, $x\mapsto(I-tB)x+tf$ is a strict contraction in the complete space). The $L^2$ pairing $J:X	o X^*$ is compact because the argument of [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]] gives $X\hookrightarrow L^2$ compact on the smooth bounded domain $A$; the original form operator is a shifted inverse composed with $I-\lambda K$, $K$ compact, so the Fredholm alternative [[thm-fredholm-alternative-for-identity-minus-compact]] (with its Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]) gives bounded invertibility once the kernel is zero. Kernel. For a homogeneous solution the imaginary part of $a(E,E)$ is $-\operatorname{Im}\langle T_RE,Eangle=0$, and the strictly positive DtN imaginary coefficients force all three outer traces of $E$ to vanish. Extending the field by the outgoing series outside $B_R$ and integrating by parts with [[cor-first-green-identity-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] gives a weak componentwise Helmholtz solution on $D$ with $H^1$ regularity on each bounded local patch, because the full traces agree across $S_R$, and it vanishes outside $B_R$. On each such patch apply [[thm-interior-h-two-regularity-for-divergence-form-equations]] with principal matrix $I$, $b=0$, $c=-k^2$, $f=0$ (equivalently $-\Delta E=k^2E$), giving $H^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The real and imaginary parts of each component then satisfy $\Delta w=-k^2w$ on the connected $D$ and vanish on its nonempty exterior open subset, so the direct local supplier [[thm-bounded-potential-weak-unique-continuation-in-three-dimensions]] makes them zero. No scalar inner Dirichlet condition is inferred from tangential PEC data, and the scalar exterior-Dirichlet lemma is not invoked in this kernel step. Hence the kernel is zero and the shifted-then-unshifted problem is boundedly invertible. Inhomogeneous data. For prescribed smooth $e_T$, give each Cartesian scalar component the Dirichlet boundary datum $(e_T)_j$ on $\partial O$ and zero on $S_R$. The weak prescribed-trace solver [[lem-em-prescribed-fractional-dirichlet-existence]] with principal coefficient $I$ and zero bulk source, followed by the scalar smooth-data upgrade [[lem-em-smooth-domain-elliptic-regularity]], supplies a smooth componentwise lift $G$ on $\overline A$ with $G|_{\partial O}=e_T$ and $G|_{S_R}=0$ (apply to real and imaginary parts). This is a genuine scalar use of B7, distinct from the inline vector mixed-boundary regularity proof. Now solve for $u\in X$ with $a(u,v)=-a(G,v)-\int_{\partial O}(\operatorname{div}_{\partial O}e_T)\overline{v_n}$; $E=G+u$ then has the prescribed tangential trace, and testing against compactly supported interior fields gives the componentwise Helmholtz equation and the stated normal relation. Regularity. At the artificial sphere the matched traces and normal derivatives make the extended field a weak Helmholtz solution across $S_R$, so [[cor-smooth-data-give-smooth-interior-solutions]] applied on bounded local patches to the constant-coefficient operator $-\Delta-k^2$ makes the matched field smooth there; no boundary theorem is used at this artificial interior surface. At $\partial O$ rotate into a smooth frame with two tangential components and one normal component; the principal part becomes a uniformly elliptic scalar principal matrix times the identity with smooth lower-order coupling, and the boundary system (two Dirichlet components and one Robin component) is complementing: in the frozen half-space a decaying principal mode $e^{i\xi\cdot y-|\xi|t}a$ with $\xi
e0$ has $a_1=a_2=0$ and $-|\xi|a_3=0$, so all amplitudes vanish, while curvature and connection terms are lower order. Supply the vector boundary argument inline, rather than treating B7's scalar public statement as a vector theorem. After the smooth frame rotation and boundary flattening, tangential shifts preserve the two zero Dirichlet component traces, while the normal component has arbitrary admissible trace. Test with $-\delta_{-h}(\eta^2\delta_h u)$ componentwise. The scalar principal matrix times the identity gives the sum of three positive gradient squares; smooth coefficient and frame commutators are lower-order $L^2$ terms bounded by Cauchy-Schwarz and Young. The differenced Robin boundary term consists of the bounded Robin coefficient times the normal quotient trace square and its smooth coefficient commutator; the collar estimate $\|w\|_{L^2(\partial O)}^2\le\delta\|
abla w\|_2^2+C_\delta\|w\|_2^2$ absorbs the first term, and trace continuity and Young bound the commutator by the same gradient bound and known $H^1$ data. This gives uniform tangential quotient-gradient bounds. Riesz identifies all mixed second derivatives in $L^2$, and the corrected component equation recovers each normal second derivative using the uniformly positive normal principal coefficient. Iterate the tangential quotient argument with differentiated smooth data and coefficient/Robin commutators, and recover remaining normal orders from the component equations; a finite boundary cover gives all orders. Local Sobolev extension/embedding then gives classical smooth representatives. This is the actual inline mixed-boundary product-space proof obligation, with two Dirichlet components and one Robin component; it is not replaced by a scalar Dirichlet-regularity citation. Divergence. The scalar $q=\operatorname{div}E$ is a smooth Helmholtz solution on $D$; the divergence identity in a boundary frame turns the inner Robin relation into $q=0$ on $\partial O$, and the outgoing component series differentiates to an outgoing $q$; [[lem-em-exterior-outgoing-scalar-uniqueness]] then gives $q=0$ on $D$. Thus $\operatorname{div}E=0$ is deduced, not presumed.

snapshot.title: Smooth boundary regularity of PEC cavity eigenfields in the declared graph completion
snapshot.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain, and let $X$ be exactly the curl/div graph-norm completion of smooth-on-the-closure fields with $
u	imes u=0$ defined in [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]]. If $u\in X$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ weakly, and $\lambda\ge0$ satisfies $\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u\cdot\operatorname{curl}v=\lambda\int_\Omega u\cdot v$ for every $v\in X$, then $u\in H^m(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ for every integer $m\ge1$ and has a $C^\infty$ representative on the closure (indeed a smooth ambient extension to a neighbourhood of the closure). For each $m$, $\|u\|_{H^m}\le C_{m,\Omega,\lambda}\|u\|_{H^1}$. The equations $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u=\lambda u$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, $
u	imes u=0$ and $\partial_
u u_n+(\operatorname{div}
u)u_n=0$ hold classically, where $u_n=u\cdot
u$ and the normal is extended constant along collar normal lines. This includes zero eigenvalues and disconnected domains; it asserts neither equality with every maximal tangential-trace realization nor smoothness of arbitrary finite-energy modal sums.
snapshot.strategy:
1. Bilinear boundary identity in the chosen completion. Write $
u$ for the outward unit normal, extend it smoothly as a unit field in a collar, put $\kappa=\operatorname{div}
u$ on the boundary, and write $u_n=u\cdot
u$. Polarizing the identity proved in [[lem-em-smooth-pec-cavity-spectral-closure]] gives, for smooth PEC $u,v$,
$$\int_\Omega(\operatorname{curl}u\cdot\operatorname{curl}v+\operatorname{div}u\operatorname{div}v)=\int_\Omega
abla u:
abla v+\int_{\partial\Omega}\kappa u_n v_n.$$
For clarity the integration-by-parts boundary term before imposing the traces is $\sum_{i,j}\int_{\partial\Omega}(
u_j u_j\partial_i v_i-
u_j u_i\partial_i v_j)$; at the boundary $u=u_n
u$, $v=v_n
u$, the tangential derivatives of $v$ and $
u\cdot\partial_i
u=0$ reduce it to $\kappa u_n v_n$. Thus the sign is positive for an outward convex sphere ($\kappa=2/R$); no convexity is assumed. The $H^1$ norm equivalence of that supplier and the bounded trace [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] extend this identity from smooth PEC approximants to every pair in the actual graph completion $X$. Since $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the assumed full-$X$ eigenidentity therefore gives
$$\int_\Omega
abla u:
abla v+\int_{\partial\Omega}\kappa u_n v_n=\lambda\int_\Omega u\cdot v\qquad(v\in X).$$
This is the weak mixed boundary identity; no classical normal derivative has yet been assumed.

2. Flattening and actual admissibility. Shrink smooth boundary charts before taking a finite cover of the compact boundary, with nested half-boxes and cutoffs away from artificial sides. In each chart choose a smooth orthonormal frame $Q=(	au_1,	au_2,
u)$ on the boundary, by normalizing a graph tangent and putting $	au_2=
u	imes	au_1$, and extend it smoothly into the collar. In flattened coordinates $(y_1,y_2,s)$ with $s>0$ inside, write $u=QU$. The $H^1$ trace has $TU_1=TU_2=0$; $TU_3$ is free. Every localized $H^1$ triple $V$ with these two zero traces and compact support away from the artificial sides pulls back to an element of the original $X$: extend $V_1,V_2$ oddly and $V_3$ evenly across $s=0$. These are $H^1$ extensions. Indeed integrating against a smooth test on both half-spaces cancels the interface term for equal one-sided traces; the odd extensions have matching traces because their traces are zero, and the even extension has matching traces automatically. This is the first-order gluing calculation in [[lem-em-dirichlet-resolvent-h-two-and-smooth-test-density]] and the half-space trace integration argument of [[thm-wkp-extension-from-a-half-space]]. Mollify with a compact kernel even in $s$; convolution preserves these parities, converges in $H^1$, and makes the first two traces exactly zero. Multiply by an even smooth cutoff equal to one on the localized support and pull back through the smooth frame and chart. Extend by zero outside the chart. The resulting fields are smooth on the closure, have $
u	imes v_j=0$ exactly, and converge to the localized field in $H^1$, hence in the curl/div graph norm. This explicitly supplies the smooth PEC approximants required by the definition of $X$. Interior compactly supported tests are obtained by ordinary mollification. This local construction is used below; no equality with an unspecified maximal tangential-trace realization is asserted.

3. The local coupled weak system. Expanding $
abla(QU)$ in the identity of step 1 and transporting the volume measure gives a real symmetric smooth principal matrix $a^{ij}$, uniformly positive on the smaller half-box, that is scalar in the three component indices. The frame derivative terms have smooth matrix coefficients and at most one derivative of $U$. Thus the local equation for all admissible triples $V$ is
$$\sum_m\int a^{ij}\partial_jU_m\partial_iV_m+\int_B eta U_3V_3=\int f\cdot V+\sum_i\int G_i\cdot\partial_iV,$$
where $B=\{s=0\}$, $ eta=\kappa J_B$ is smooth (possibly signed), $f=\lambda JU+\sum_i C_i\partial_iU+C_0U\in L^2$, and $G_i=B_iU\in H^1$ for smooth matrix coefficients $C_i,C_0,B_i$; $J$ and $J_B$ are the positive volume and surface densities. This follows directly by expanding the finite products: the only two differentiated factors produce the scalar $a^{ij}$ because $Q^TQ=I$; terms with a derivative of $Q$ on the test factor enter $G$, and those with a derivative of $Q$ on the solution factor enter $f$. Multipliers obey [[lem-cutoff-difference-quotient-commutator-estimate]]. More generally allow a boundary datum $\int_B hV_3$ with $h\in H^1(B)$ for the induction below. Localization $Z=\eta U$ has the same principal and Robin terms and exactly $f_Z=\eta f+\sum_i G_i\partial_i\eta-\sum_{i,j}a^{ij}\partial_jU\partial_i\eta$, $G_{Z,i}=\eta G_i+\sum_j a^{ij}U\partial_j\eta$, and $h_Z=\eta h$. In particular the divergence-type cutoff/frame terms are retained rather than silently assigning zero conormal data.

4. Tangential mixed $H^2$ estimate. Let $k=1,2$, set $W=\delta_h^k U=(U(y+he_k,s)-U(y,s))/h$, and test with $V=-\delta_{-h}^k(\eta^2W)$ on a nested patch. For each fixed small $h$, its first two traces vanish; step 2 makes its pullback an admissible element of $X$ by actual smooth PEC approximation. Discrete integration by parts and the shifted product rule give the principal term $\sum_m\int\eta^2 a^{ij}(x+he_k)\partial_jW_m\partial_iW_m\ge\alpha\|\eta
abla W\|_2^2$. The other principal terms involve $\delta_h a$, $
abla\eta$, $
abla U$ and $W$ and are bounded by $\epsilon\|\eta
abla W\|_2^2+C_\epsilon\|U\|_{H^1}^2$ on the larger patch. The elementary line formula $\delta_h U=\int_0^1\partial_kU(x+the_k)dt$, valid on a.e. ACL line, and Cauchy--Schwarz in $t$ followed by Fubini give $\|W\|_2\le C\|\partial_kU\|_2$ on the enlarged patch; it also bounds $\|\delta_{-h}(\eta^2W)\|_2$ by $C(\|\eta
abla W\|_2+\|W\|_2)$. Hence the $f$ term is bounded without differentiating $f$. Transfer the quotient in the $G$ pairing to $G$; $\|\delta_hG\|_2\le C\|G\|_{H^1}$ gives the same bound. On $B$ the exact quotient of the Robin product gives $\int_B eta(y+h)\eta^2|W_3|^2+\int_B(\delta_h eta)U_3\eta^2W_3$. The normal-line proof in G3 gives the localized trace estimate $\|Tz\|_2^2\le\epsilon\|
abla z\|_2^2+C_\epsilon\|z\|_2^2$. It absorbs the first term even when $ eta$ has either sign; bounded $\delta_h eta$, $\|TU_3\|_2\le C\|U\|_{H^1}$ and Young bound the second in the same way. The extra $h$ pairing transfers to $\delta_h h$ and is bounded by $\|h\|_{H^1(B)}\|T(\eta^2W_3)\|_2$, again absorbed by the trace estimate and Young. Choosing the finitely many epsilons small relative to $\alpha$ yields
$$\|\eta
abla\delta_h^kU\|_2\le C(\|U\|_{H^1}+\|f\|_2+\|G\|_{H^1}+\|h\|_{H^1(B)}),$$
uniformly for small $h$. These estimates apply to all three components and explicitly bound the coupled lower-order and Robin terms; a scalar Dirichlet theorem has not been substituted for this system.

5. Recover normal derivatives. From the last bound each distributional tangential derivative of $\partial_iU_m$ is $L^2$: for a smooth test $\psi$ its pairing is the limit of $\int\delta_h^k(\partial_iU_m)\psi$, a bounded $L^2$ functional, represented by an $L^2$ class (Hilbert Riesz, available through the variational supplier in G3). Interior quotient tests give the same conclusion away from the boundary. The interior equation is $-\partial_i(a^{ij}\partial_jU_m)=f_m-\partial_iG_{i,m}$. Therefore
$$a^{33}\partial_{33}U_m=\partial_iG_{i,m}-f_m-\sum_{(i,j)
e(3,3)}a^{ij}\partial_{ij}U_m-\sum_{i,j}(\partial_i a^{ij})\partial_jU_m.$$
Every term on the right is $L^2$, and $a^{33}\ge\alpha>0$, so all three normal second derivatives are $L^2$. This proves local $H^2$ with a bound on a smaller patch. It does not require a pre-existing classical Robin derivative.

6. Full bootstrap with boundary commutators. Suppose $U\in H^{r+1}$ on the larger patch, $r\ge1$. Its actual lower-order data satisfy $f\in H^r$ and $G\in H^{r+1}$, since the equation's eigenvalue term is $\lambda JU$ and all coefficients are smooth; no initially smooth right-hand side is presumed. For a tangential multi-index $\alpha$ of order $r$, put $Z=D_y^\alpha U\in H^1$. Its first two traces are still zero. To justify trace commutation, extend any localized $H^{r+1}$ class by the integer-order half-space extension [[thm-wkp-extension-from-a-half-space]], mollify in that norm, and use the continuous $H^1$ trace for every derivative of order at most $r$; the smooth tangential trace identity passes to the limit. Apply tangential integration by parts to the weak system of step 3. Its principal term remains $a^{ij}\partial_j Z_m\partial_iV_m$, its boundary principal term remains $ eta Z_3V_3$, its bulk datum is $D_y^\alpha f\in L^2$, and its divergence-type datum is
$$\widetilde G_i=D_y^\alpha G_i-\sum_{0<\gamma\le\alpha}{\alpha\choose\gamma}(D_y^\gamma a^{ij})\partial_jD_y^{\alpha-\gamma}U\in H^1.$$
The boundary commutator is $\widetilde h=-\sum_{0<\gamma\le\alpha}{\alpha\choose\gamma}(D_y^\gamma eta)T D_y^{\alpha-\gamma}U_3\in H^1(B)$. Indeed $|\alpha-\gamma|\le r-1$, so the indicated derivative of $U$ is $H^2$; its trace and each tangential derivative trace are $L^2$ by the $H^1$ trace and its just-proved commutation. This proves the claimed $H^1(B)$ bound without assuming a stronger trace theorem. Step 2 again makes localized tests for $Z$ admissible by smooth PEC approximation; differentiation of the weak identity is justified first by difference quotients and then distributional limits. Steps 4--5 give $Z\in H^2$, controlling derivatives of total order $r+2$ with at most two normal derivatives. For the remaining derivatives, differentiate the normal-recovery equation of step 5 and induct on the number of normal derivatives at this fixed total order. The non-$(3,3)$ principal terms have strictly fewer normal derivatives; all differentiated coefficient terms use derivatives of $U$ of order at most $r+1$, and differentiated $f$ and $\operatorname{div}G$ have that same available order. Dividing by positive $a^{33}$ recovers the next normal derivative. Thus $U\in H^{r+2}$. Use nested patches for each finite order and the finite boundary/interior cover to obtain $u\in H^m(\Omega)$ for every integer $m$, with $\|u\|_{H^m}\le C_{m,\Omega,\lambda}\|u\|_{H^1}$; no estimate uniform in $\lambda$ is asserted.

7. Classical conclusion. For each $j$ choose $m>j+3/2$ and apply [[thm-extension-theorem-for-bounded-smooth-domains]] and [[thm-higher-order-sobolev-embedding]] componentwise. They yield continuous derivatives through order $j$ on the closure, compatible for different $j$ by weak derivative uniqueness and continuity on the interior. All jets therefore have continuous one-sided boundary limits. The fixed smooth extension [[lem-em-parameter-preserving-smooth-extension-on-a-smooth-domain]] applied to the constant-in-time field gives one actual smooth ambient representative near the entire closure, rather than unrelated finite-order extensions. The interior variational equation gives $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u=\lambda u$ pointwise, and the tangential trace is classically zero. Now integration by parts in step 1 with arbitrary smooth compactly supported normal boundary traces, admissible by step 2, gives $\partial_
u u_n+\kappa u_n=0$ pointwise. The unit-normal collar extension ensures $\partial_
u u_n=(\partial_
u u)\cdot
u$ when the normal is extended constant along its normal lines. This agrees with the classical identity $\operatorname{div}u=\partial_
u u_n+\kappa u_n$ for zero tangential trace. The argument covers $\lambda=0$, disconnected smooth domains, and every topology allowed by G3; it makes no smoothness assertion for arbitrary finite-energy modal sums. Full AC is carried from G3, the trace, extension, Hilbert and Sobolev suppliers.
